p.t: The best option is that the **supplier ships on its own account**.
An account is the supplier's login with the carrier (the shipping company).
With this option you get **one invoice** (one bill). The supplier also handles returns, loss and breakage.

**Ask suppliers this first**, before you arrange any other shipping option.
**Always ask** suppliers to ship on their own accounts when possible.
Suppliers get **better rates** because they ship a lot. Volume means how many packages they send. Suppliers can also handle tracking issues (problems following a package).
Give your UPS or FedEx account (large shipping companies) only if the supplier **clearly cannot** ship from its own.
Ship through the supplier's own shipping account **whenever possible**. Suppliers ship high volumes and often get bulk discounts (lower prices for large quantities), which lower the cost (2025).
Have the supplier ship from its own carrier account when possible, because suppliers ship more and get **better discounts** (2025).
If a supplier **will not** ship on its account, the store must send a bill of lading for freight shipments. Freight means large, heavy shipments.
A bill of lading is the shipping paper that lists the goods and where they go (2025).
Use the supplier's shipping account. **Do not plan for freight carriers** unless the supplier refuses to ship from its account.
Ask suppliers to ship on their own shipping account whenever possible, because it **reduces liability** (legal responsibility for problems).
It also **simplifies operations** (how the business runs day to day).
If a supplier refuses, using **your own freight account through a freight broker** (a middleman who books freight for you) is still workable.
Prefer suppliers who ship on their own account. They **bill shipping on the invoice** and handle damage claims and replacements. Take this option whenever it is available.

Prefer suppliers who ship from their own accounts, because it keeps operations simpler.
**Bill of lading shipments are still acceptable** when a supplier requires them.

**Set shipments** to go out on the supplier's account by default.
If the supplier will not, get a freight quote (a price offer) and a bill of lading. Have the shipment billed to the supplier.
Ship orders on the supplier's account **whenever possible**. The supplier then handles damage insurance claims (requests for payment after damage).

If it will not, ship on your own account. This is also common.
Ship on the supplier's own account, with the supplier billing the store, **whenever possible**.
Use this approach to keep operations simple.
Ship on the supplier's own account when it offers published or discounted UPS rates (price lists).

Ask whether the supplier has a **discounted rate sheet** (a price list) for its carrier account.
Prefer suppliers with **short shipping times**.
Ship on the supplier's own account **whenever possible**, since this is smoother for every order.
Your shipping page can list all carriers you may use. Orders from different carriers are **not a problem**.
Ship on the supplier's account by default, and count the shipping fee as a **cost per order**.
Offering free shipping to customers means the store pays this fee to the supplier. So it is not actually free for the business. In the example it was **100 USD per order**.
Suppliers either ship on their own account and charge you for shipping, or they ship on your account.
Your preferred option is for the supplier to ship on its account and **bill you for shipping**. If it does not allow that, you ship on your own account.
Shipping on the supplier's account makes it **faster to print labels** (shipping stickers) and ship the same day.
It also makes claims simpler if an item is damaged or lost **in transit** (on the way to the customer). The supplier can file the claim and send a replacement quickly.

Ask suppliers which carriers their largest retailers use. Shipping on a supplier's business account usually gives **bulk pricing**.

A foreign manufacturer is acceptable if its products are **stored in a US warehouse** (a storage building) (2023).

Some suppliers, **roughly 5 to 10 percent**, require the seller to ship on their own account.

**Supplier's account**
Who bills the shipping: Supplier bills you for shipping, usually as one invoice with the product

Invoice: One invoice (product plus shipping)
Damage and replacement claims: Supplier files the claim and sends a replacement quickly

**Your own account**
Who bills the shipping: Supplier charges only the product; the carrier bills the shipping separately
Invoice: Two bills: supplier for product, carrier for shipping
Damage and replacement claims: You are liable for overage claims (charges for extra weight or size), and in-transit damage must be claimed from the carrier

Shipping on the supplier's account keeps damage and replacement claims **with the supplier** (2024).

p.t: Using your own carrier account
**Do not open** a shipping carrier account before contacting suppliers.
Ask which carrier the supplier recommends. Suppliers know which carriers already collect at their warehouse (a storage building) at the best rates.

For standard UPS or FedEx shipments, **create your own account** with each carrier.
Give the supplier your account numbers, so it ships on your account rather than its own.
Create a **free** UPS or FedEx account online.
Share your account number with suppliers. They use their own access to create shipping labels and charge the cost to your account.

This requires **almost no effort** from you once set up.
**Setup for small parcels (small packages) when a supplier will not ship on its own account (UPS or FedEx):**

1. Open a **free account** with ups.com or fedex.com.
2. Send your carrier account number to the supplier.

3. The supplier creates the shipping labels on your account for each order.
**Shipping options when a supplier does not ship on its own account:**
1. Give the supplier a FedEx or UPS account number so it ships on your account. Both can be opened free online.

2. If that is not possible, ask the supplier which **freight carrier or freight broker** it recommends.
3. Partner with the recommended carrier or broker for those shipments.

4. For each customer order, place the order with the supplier **after the sale**.
5. Then use the chosen shipping method.
**When a supplier will not ship on its own account:**
1. Ask the supplier which shipping company or freight broker it recommends. It already works with other retailers and knows which carrier handles most of its orders.

2. Contact the recommended carrier or broker.
3. Set up the account or partnership with that company for your shipments.

**Choosing a method with a supplier that does not ship on its account (2023):**
1. Contact the supplier and ask about its **preferred shipping method**.
2. If items are large and heavy, use a freight broker via freightcenter.com. The supplier may provide a freight account, or you create your own.

Ask suppliers who they **recommend as a shipping company**. Do not just ask whether they ship on their own account.

Ask which carriers the supplier recommends and which large retailers it uses.

**Opening a business account for a better rate:**
1. Ask the supplier which carrier its top retailers use for shipping.

2. Contact that carrier and **open a business account** in your own name.
3. Tell the carrier where you ship from, and that current pricing is **not competitive**.

4. Ask for a **discount** on the account.
5. Expect discounts to **grow with shipping volume**.
Template for asking a carrier for a discount:
Hi [carrier contact name], This is [your name] with [business name]. We have opened a business account with [carrier name] and we ship our products from [ship-from city, state].
The current shipping pricing is not competitive for us. Is there any discount you can apply to our account?
We expect our shipping volume to grow, so we would also like to know how discounts increase as we ship more. Thank you, [your name] [business name] [phone number]
Shipping discounts from carriers are usually based on **volume** (how many packages you send) (2023).
Higher volumes through a carrier, or shipping through a supplier who ships a lot on its own account, generally produce the **best rates** (2023).
Shipping services that charge a fee on top of carrier rates are only useful for stores with their own warehouse and **high shipping volume**.
For drop-ship stores, these services are generally **not worth the cost**.

Before accepting a third-party group shipping discount (a deal from a company outside you and the carrier), **compare** its rates against your actual shipping lanes. Lanes are the routes your packages travel.
Some lanes may get better rates while others get worse. Do not assume a group deal is a good deal for everyone.

p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: For items that are not large, heavy or freight, use the carrier the supplier prefers. This is usually UPS or FedEx (2025).

Large, heavy items need a **different carrier** (2025).
Carrier choice for small parcels in Australia: Couriers Please, Sendle and eParcel were recommended.
**Compare** their rates and delivery times before choosing one for a store.
In Australia, many brands rely on Australia Post. It is **required by government to deliver nationwide** (across the whole country).
A hybrid setup (a mix of two services) with StarTrack, which Australia Post owns, can offer a **branded tracking page** (a tracking page with your store's look) on top of the carrier.

Pirate Ship is mentioned as a good option for small parcels (2025).
Someone recommended it from experience, but had **not used it personally** (2025).

Pirate Ship is reported to be **cheaper than UPS** for small parcels (2023).
Its insurance is provided through a third party (2023).
Compare its rates against your own UPS quote **before switching** (2023).

Check shipping costs with a supplier's **shipping calculator** (a tool that shows the price) before committing.
International UPS shipping is typically **very expensive**.

If the cost looks unreasonable to you, customers will likely see it the same way.
Sales reps (salespeople) at supplier brands are the **best source for shipping advice**.
Ask which carrier they prefer, what pricing they get, and how their largest online retailers ship.
Before you use the same carrier as a supplier's other retailers, **check its label status**. Label status shows whether the shipping label has been created and scanned.

If a supplier has a label pending status with FedEx for more than about **24 hours**, call the carrier.
Ask whether the delay is on the supplier's side or the carrier's side.

If a supplier **marks up** shipping above its real cost (adds extra money on top), ship on your own account (2024).
Do not pay the markup.

p.t: If a supplier offers a better price when you handle shipping yourself, ask whether it means you buy the **stock in advance** (buy products before customers order).

Or ask whether it means you pay for shipping.
If you ship with your own UPS or FedEx account, or through a freight broker's bill of lading, this can **save money**.

Ask the supplier whether it can use **the same shipping method** you select (2023).
If the price still does not match, shipping on your own account is the **next step** (2023).

**Matching the carrier price with your own UPS account (2023):**
1. Ask the supplier to ship with **the same shipping method** you select, so the price matches your quote.

2. If it cannot match it, open a **free UPS account** for your business.
3. Give the supplier your UPS account number.
4. The supplier creates each shipment in UPS and enters your account number in the billing section.

5. UPS bills you for the shipping. You pay the supplier only for the cost of the goods.
Template for querying a supplier's higher shipping price (2023):
Hi [Supplier contact name], we were reviewing the quotes for our shipments and noticed yours are substantially higher than the ones we get from UPS.
Just wanted to make sure you are choosing the same shipping method, or are we missing something here? Could you check whether you can use the shipping method we select so the price matches?
If not, we would like to ship on our own UPS account, so please use our account number [UPS account number] when you create shipments. [Your name] [Company name]
Supplier **surcharges** (extra fees) for shipping on their own account are a reason to compare with self-arranged carrier quotes before accepting.
For example, a surcharge may be **5 dollars** on regular items and **25 dollars** on large items.
Shipping on the supplier's account versus on the seller's account works like this. When the supplier ships on its own account, it charges the product plus shipping in **one invoice**.
When the seller ships on its own UPS or FedEx account, the supplier charges only the product. The carrier bills the shipping separately.

p.t: **Negotiating shipping costs with a supplier:**
1. Bring **real numbers** to the supplier. Include the number of sales, where orders shipped, shipping costs, and the **margin** (profit left per sale) you are left with.
2. Ask whether the supplier can ship through its preferred carriers on its own account, which often gives better rates.
3. Ask for **incentivized pricing** (special prices offered to encourage a deal) or a **wholesale discount** (a lower price for buying in bulk for resale).
The product then becomes profitable for both sides.
4. If the supplier ships through freight, get separate freight quotes from freight brokers. Compare them with the supplier's rate.
Template for asking a supplier to cover shipping on its account and cut costs:
Hi [Supplier name], last year we spent about [98,000] with you on shipping and fulfillment.
Your shipping volume is likely higher than ours, so could you check whether your freight accounts or carrier rates can cover our orders at a lower cost?
Our target for next year is about [75,000], and I would like to agree on a plan to reach it. Could we set up a call this week to review the rates? Thank you, [Your name].
Some suppliers do not coordinate shipping, or their shipping is **too expensive**. So the store may use a separate freight provider such as UPS.

In that case, **product cost and shipping cost must be tracked separately**.
Both need to be compared against the supplier's pricing.
Record each supplier's shipping and fulfilment details. Fulfilment means packing and sending orders.
These details help an assistant arrange pickups. Include **supplier pickup times**, **warehouse hours**, the **contact person**, and which carriers collect from the supplier's area.
Insurance, damage and claims
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: **Insure every shipment.** Insurance is the baseline protection (the minimum safety net), regardless of which carrier is used.
Insurance stops occasional damage from costing the store money.
Insure every shipment, whether the supplier ships it or you ship from your own shipping account (2025).
This way, damaged or lost goods can be replaced **without an out-of-pocket loss** (money you pay from your own pocket) (2025).

Insurance is selected as an option when the shipment is created (2025).
Shipments sent to customers should be insured against **loss and transit damage**.

Suppliers usually insure shipments made on their own accounts.
Insure shipments yourself **only if damage is rare** with that supplier (2024).
If the supplier ships on its own account, it handles claims (2024).
Before paying extra for specialized shipping on fragile goods (easily broken items), check each supplier's products for complaints:

1. Search Google for the supplier's name and product names together with "reviews".
2. Look for **repeated** mentions of returns, refunds or damage from other stores' customers.
3. If no clear pattern appears, ship with a recommended carrier and insure every shipment.

4. Only use costlier specialized shippers if damage remains a **recurring problem**.
Check the carrier's insurance terms before relying on insurance.
Some policies exclude parcels shipped in manufacturer boxes printed with product names or SKUs (product codes). This can lead to **denied damage claims**.
Insurance is covered by the supplier when it ships on its account. The store can then focus on tracking the claim and the replacement.
Tracking and multi-Supplier shipments
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Require suppliers to send a **tracking number** (a code to follow the package) when an order ships.
A supplier that offers no tracking at all is a risk. Ask it to at least reply to purchase orders (orders you place with the supplier) with tracking numbers.
In-stock orders should have tracking information sent **within 24 hours** of the order leaving the warehouse.

If the customer has none after **four business days**, they should follow up by email.
Customers accept **multiple packages** if they receive tracking numbers (2024).
When customers order products that ship from multiple suppliers, send tracking information for **each shipment** as it ships separately (2024).
Handling a multi-item order shipped from different suppliers:
1. Expect the items to ship **separately from different warehouses**, and tell the customer this is normal.
2. When part of an order ships, enter the tracking number in the Shopify order backend (the admin page where store orders are managed). Enter it for **only the products that shipped**.
3. Keep the customer updated so each separate shipment is expected and understood.
When a store's products come from several suppliers, supplier-specific shipping costs can make some products **unprofitable**.

Check shipping cost and the supplier's location **before deciding where to advertise**.
Free tracked shipping instead of standard shipping can increase trust.

It can also reduce **checkout drop-off** (customers leaving before they pay).
Weekly shipments for bulk ordering:
1. Collect all orders placed **Monday to Friday**.
2. On Friday, batch-ship (send as one group) all week's orders to DHL (a shipping company) in **one consolidated shipment** (combined into one).
3. Do this instead of sending individual drops.
Regional assignment of suppliers **reduces shipping times**. Instead of one centralized warehouse (one main storage site), assign suppliers by region (2025).
For example, Northeast suppliers handle Northeast orders, and Southeast suppliers handle Southeast orders (2025).
This speeds delivery **without increasing costs** (2025).

p.t: Free shipping and pricing it in
Offer **free shipping** on all products as the base option.
p.h: Deciding whether to build shipping into the price

p.t: The business pays the carrier (the shipping company) for each parcel.
Rates are checked after orders come in. They are not worked out at checkout (the payment step).
Free shipping is paid out of the seller's own margin (the money kept per sale after costs).
Sell a product under a free-shipping threshold (the minimum order amount for free shipping) for example under 3,500 **only if** the margin covers the shipping cost.
Shipping fees vary by supplier (the company that ships your products) (2025).
Because the store offers free shipping on everything, build the shipping cost into product prices.
Each order must still leave a minimum of **25 percent** net profit (money left after all costs).
If a supplier cannot be priced to cover shipping, **limit** its products in advertising to nearby regions.
If you charge shipping at checkout, decide whether to build it into the price or charge it separately.
To decide, **check** what the top 2 or 3 competitors do for the same brand (2023).
Free shipping is the usual standard in these niches (product groups), so it does not set you apart.
**Check** what the top two to five competitors charge for shipping, and price your products to match.
Deciding whether to build shipping into the price (continued)

p.t: Those stores are your direct rivals on Google Shopping (Google's product listing ads) (2024).
Free shipping from suppliers is a plus when you launch a store with a few suppliers (2024).

When a supplier says shipping is free, **confirm** whether the shipping cost is built into the product price.
This changes the margin calculation.

Passing international shipping costs to the buyer is possible only if the final price still works for the product.
Shipping should **never cost more than the product itself**.
For heavy items, avoid real-time shipping calculation (a shipping cost worked out live in the store).
Instead, build the shipping cost into the product price and offer free shipping, **if the product is still profitable**.

Shipping that a supplier charges directly to the customer can be handled in one of two ways.
Option one: **add the cost** to the product price.
Option two: create a separate Shopify (the online store software) shipping profile (a set of shipping rules) for that supplier's products (2024).

Some suppliers require the seller to create and send a shipping label (the printed postage for a parcel).
In that case, the store pays that shipping cost directly.
For heavy items, **check this cost before listing**. It can exceed the margin and make the product unprofitable (2024).
A competitor may advertise free international shipping for a bulky or heavy product. Cross-border (between countries) shipping of large or heavy goods is very costly.
There are two possible explanations. Either the cost is built into an expensive price, or the seller stocks the same product in warehouses in both countries.

A claim of truly free shipping only works for very high-priced, small items.
**Check which explanation applies** before copying the model.
Free shipping is excluded for Hawaii and Alaska, because it is too expensive to offer for free.
Calculating an average shipping cost (2018 method)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Note each approved supplier's shipping origin (where it ships from) and where your customers are located, for example the share of sales per state.
2. Ask each supplier for shipping quotes (price offers) for its most popular product to those regions, ideally while applying for approval.
3. Calculate an average shipping cost per product. Weight it by the share of your business in each region, for example a 50 percent split between two regions.
4. Add that average into the product price. Do not mark the price up more for shipping.
5. Check that the resulting net margin still meets the 25 percent minimum while free shipping is offered.
6. If the margin still does not cover shipping for a supplier, **limit** that supplier's products in advertising to nearby regions (see geo-targeting, showing ads only in chosen regions).

Example: a stand-up paddle board costs about 50 dollars to ship within the same state.
The same board costs about 150 dollars to ship from a supplier in a distant state.
If half of the customers are in each zone, the average of **100 dollars** is the figure to build into the price.
If a product's shipping cost can use up nearly all of its net profit per order, **do not sell it to the expensive regions**.

For example, 150 dollars of profit against 150 dollars of shipping is too little.
This situation should be rare.
If a supplier cannot quote shipping for individual items, **ask for package specifications** (the size and weight of each item and box).

Ask for them in a spreadsheet or CSV (a plain spreadsheet file).
Then estimate costs from those numbers.

p.t: Hi [Supplier name], we have been approved and are preparing our store. Most of our customers are in [State A], about [X]% of our business, and we also sell to [State B].
What would it cost to ship your most popular product, [product name], to a [State A] address and to a [State B] address? Please include the package weight and dimensions with each quote.

Estimating a typical shipping cost from a supplier's warehouse (2025):
1. Get the zip code (US postal code) of the supplier's warehouse.
2. Request sample shipping quotes from that warehouse to several random US zip codes. For example, New Jersey to New York, Florida, Texas and California.

3. **Average the quotes** to estimate the typical shipping cost per order.
4. Use this average, not a single quote, when calculating margins.

**Track** the shipping cost against the margin before you cut prices.
Shipping costs can quickly erase margin on heavy items.
So apply the calculated average, not a single quote, when setting prices.
Shipping costs can jump sharply when a product moves into a higher shipping size class (a size group carriers use to set prices).

Even a one-inch increase in length can matter.
Ask suppliers for the dimensions that define each shipping class.

Also ask which packing materials they use.
Do this **before deciding** how to box or group products.

Enter accurate product shipping dimensions for every item, especially large ones.
Wrong sizes can make shipping costs higher than needed.
Enter package sizes such as box dimensions in Shopify so that carrier-calculated rates (rates the carrier works out) are accurate.
Branded mailer boxes (shipping boxes printed with a logo) can be sourced from a friend's business in exchange for free packaging.

The parcel then carries that business's branding as part of the arrangement.
This lowers packaging cost in the early phase of a small brand.

p.t: Shopify setup: locations, rates, zones and profiles

Go to **Settings > Locations** and keep the default location unchanged.
Do not add supplier addresses.
The location represents the business's billing location, not the suppliers.
In Shopify, enter your business address or main fulfillment location as the shipping origin address (where parcels leave from).

With free shipping (no shipping cost charged to the customer), this address does not affect rate calculations.
It is mainly for documentation.
Go to **Settings > Shipping and delivery**.
Create one domestic shipping rate (a rate for orders inside the country), with the country United States and the rate Free shipping.

Customers then see Free Shipping at checkout.
This setup applies when the store offers free shipping.

In the shipping rate editor, the Offer free shipping option makes a rate free.
Checkout then shows the rate name with FREE instead of a price.
A paid rate uses rate type Flat (one fixed price) with a Price field.
The Shipping labels section in Settings > Shipping and delivery lets you buy discounted shipping labels and manage preferred carriers.

The Carrier accounts section lets you connect an existing carrier account (your own shipping company login).
Its own rates are then used at checkout.

Settings > Shipping and delivery > Additional delivery methods offers Local delivery and Pickup in store.
These are options alongside regular shipping.
The Sender name on shipping labels field is in the same section.

p.t: Shopify shipping profiles sort which products ship from which regions or suppliers.
Multiple profiles let you assign Supplier A products to specific states and Supplier B products to others (2025).
The Shipping profiles section has an Add custom profile button.
Use it to create an extra profile for specific products. That profile can have its own zones (regions with their own rates) and rates.

Products not assigned to a custom profile stay in the General profile.
The General profile is labeled as covering all products not in other profiles.

Go to Settings > Shipping and delivery > General profile > Packages.
Enter package sizes there, so that carrier-calculated rates are accurate.
The Packages field sits in the same profile view as the shipping zones and estimated delivery dates.
Different suppliers have different shipping speeds and need different delivery windows.

Create **separate product templates** for each supplier group.
Assign the correct template to products.
Set estimated delivery to match that supplier's actual timeline.
Set a shipping profile for each supplier that lists its made-to-order lead time (see the made-to-order section below).
The Customs information section in a Shopify product has two fields.

The first is Country/Region of origin. This is usually where the product is made.
The second is an HS code (an international product code, found by searching a keyword).
Border officers use these fields to calculate import duties (taxes on goods entering a country).

The fields also appear on the customs forms (border paperwork) printed during fulfillment.
Demo products can skip this section.

**Exclude Alaska and Hawaii from the free shipping offer (2021)**

For them, set the freight option to **yes**.
See regional supplier assignment and shipping profiles above.
p.h: Regional supplier assignment and multi-state profiles

p.t: When a supplier stocks both a US warehouse and a China warehouse, US stock usually ships faster to US customers.

**Route orders to US stock** where the product is available.
Compare delivery times on both warehouses before choosing.
Unsupported countries
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: For a country your supplier will not ship to, **check the real shipping cost** before selling.
Enter the item's dimensions, weight and destination address to check it.
Shipping surcharge test (an extra fee added to the price) for a country your supplier will not ship to:
1. Track the actual extra cost per order. For example, track the cost of reshipping through a relay address (a forwarding address in another place), and calculate the average.
2. Add a surcharge for that country at about that average. Example: average cost $100, surcharge set to $120.
3. Watch whether orders continue. If they do, the surcharge covers the cost. If they stop, you avoided losing money on shipping.

Fast delivery sells more in markets like Spain.
Delivering within **about 48 hours** helps conversion (the share of visitors who buy).
Cheap prices matter most for buyers there.
Cross-border export (sending goods between countries): before you ship products from suppliers in other countries, **ask each supplier** how it handles export.

The process varies by supplier.
For products made abroad with long delivery times, state three things on the product page.
Say where the product is made. Say what happens after the order. Give the estimated delivery time, for example four weeks.
Clear disclosure prevents most complaints.
Handling time, transit time and delivery estimates

Handling time is the number of days from the customer's order to the item being processed and ready to ship.
It is not the shipping duration.

Dropshippers (sellers whose supplier ships to the customer) do not control this.
So a **single-day** handling time is risky. Use a window (a range of days) instead.
Delivery expectations should separate three figures, each stated in business days: average handling time, average transit time (time on the road) and typical total delivery time.

Giving all three figures sets accurate expectations for large purchases.
It also reduces refund requests caused by surprise delays.
Delivery windows by source
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t:
The sources give different windows. Each one applies to a different supplier and niche.
**Source B, dropshipping store**

Handling time: 1 to 3 days, Monday to Friday only
Transit time: 1 to 7 days, adjustable over time
Total delivery: Not stated

Applies when: Most dropshipping stores; very few suppliers ship on weekends
**Source B, in-stock orders**
Handling time: Typically 1 to 3 business days

Transit time: 1 to 6 business days after shipment
Total delivery: Not stated
Applies when: In-stock items

**Source A, starting placeholders (no year)**
Handling time: 3 to 5 business days
Transit time: 3 to 7 business days

Total delivery: 7 to 12 business days
Applies when: Until supplier timelines are known; can be changed later
**Source A, shipping policy**

Handling time: Dispatch 1 to 2 days, depending on each supplier's cut-off
Transit time: 1 to 7 days (up to two days dispatch on the long end)

Total delivery: Not stated
Applies when: Standard parcels; freight takes longer
**Source A, shipping policy**

Handling time: Dispatch within 48 business hours
Transit time: 2 to 5 business days
Total delivery: Not stated

Applies when: General policy average; supplier-specific times go on each product page
**Source A, example supplier**

Handling time: Supplier needs 2 to 3 days, stated as ships within 72 hours
Transit time: Tracking follows by email
Total delivery: Not stated

Applies when: Per-supplier product page, when a supplier needs 2 to 3 days
**Do not promise** delivery times that are too fast or too slow.

Overpromising leads to angry customers when delivery is late.
Very long transit times, such as 20 to 30 days on average, put buyers off.
The estimated delivery date shown to customers is calculated from three things: the order time (before or after the order cutoff, the daily deadline), the handling time and the transit time.
Google adjusts the estimate automatically when a public holiday falls within the delivery period.
Delivery windows by source (continued)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: The order cutoff time in a Merchant Center shipping service (Google's product feed tool) is optional.
If you use it, set it to the business's local time zone (the clock time where the business is).

For example, use 5 PM in GMT+10 for a business in Brisbane, Australia.
Most suppliers should **dispatch orders within one to two days** (send them out).

Learn each supplier's daily order cut-off time.
Orders placed before the cut-off ship the same day. Later orders ship the next day.

Same-day shipping can be offered as an upsell (an extra paid option) only if the supplier can ship by a fixed cutoff time.
For example, the order must be placed by noon Eastern time.

Suppliers that ship in around three days cannot support this offer without that cutoff.
Record each supplier's time from order submission to dispatch.

State it on that supplier's product pages.
For example, if a supplier needs 2 to 3 days, tell customers the item ships within 72 hours.

Also tell them that tracking follows by email.
**Add processing days** to the advertised shipping window.
Counting only the advertised shipping days with a supplier underestimates delivery time.
Long processing times with a supplier like CJ (CJ Dropshipping, a supplier platform) can lead to angry customers.

This is especially true around holidays or long weekends.
Carrier delivery estimates can shift by several days, or even a week, during the holiday catch-up period.

This is especially true with domestic shipping (inside the country).
Set customer expectations around a range.

Keep the tracking ETA (estimated arrival time) visible.
Do not promise one fixed delivery date.
Keep the estimate for lead time (time from order to ready) or shipping visible and clear on the product page.
Delivery windows by source (continued)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Customers usually accept longer delivery times when they are stated openly.

Delivery information can be shown as an estimated date range or as typical shipping time.
Choose the format that fits your products.

Custom-made items need different wording than items shipped within 48 hours.
Put a general average shipping time in the shipping policy.

For example: dispatch within 48 business hours and delivery within 2 to 5 business days.
Add the supplier-specific lead time on each product page's shipping tab.

Customers used to fast delivery may see 10 business days as slow.
So a 14-day supplier route still carries refund risk.

Delivery times of **4 to 6 weeks** cause refunds and lasting problems.
Avoid those routes.

Fashion dropshipping: keep communication with the supplier very good.
Make sure products deliver within **about 10 days**.
Slow delivery increases refund and dispute (a customer complaint to the payment company) risk.

Long shipping times can kill viral momentum (the fast spread of interest in a product).
Standard dropshipping delivery can take around three weeks.

By then, buyers and the seller have often lost interest.
When shipping times are a problem, check eBay (an online marketplace) for the same product.
Consider paying extra for faster shipping.
Paying more on CJ Dropshipping or AliExpress (an online marketplace) has sometimes produced delivery within about one week.

Customers respond well to fast shipping.
So choose suppliers and fulfillment (the packing and sending of orders) that **prioritize short delivery times**.
Fast delivery is a competitive advantage in dropshipping.
Claims about speed
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t:
Claims of same-day or one-day shipping on dropshipping stores are usually unrealistic.
Many stores show three to five days shipping.

**Plan delivery times** around realistic supplier shipping times, not competitor claims.
A competitor stated that most orders are dispatched within **2 hours** of being placed.

This dispatch-time claim works as a delivery promise.
Record stated dispatch times, together with tracking and shipping claims, in the features and deliverables column.
Lead times of 3 to 6 weeks are acceptable **only if** your top 2 to 3 competitors have the same lead time.
p.h: Lead times and long supplier routes

p.t:
If competitors ship in 24 hours and you ship in 3 to 6 weeks at the same price, customers will buy from competitors.
Clearly display the lead time on product pages.

Confirm it with customers after order placement (2024).
A supplier with a lead time of several weeks is not automatically a problem.

That is true if it is standard in the niche.
Show the delivery time on the product pages, for example two to three weeks, so customers know what to expect.

Long shipping times are a problem only when they are not standard for the niche.
In custom-made product niches, customers accept longer waits.

But the custom order process should be clear to buyers before they purchase.
Prefer suppliers with short shipping times.

See the supplier-selection rules above.
CJ offers about six or seven different shipping methods.

Shipping time depends on the supplier and the method agreed.
CJ Sensitive shipping to Australia takes about 7 to 15 days.
The speaker used it as the default shipping method for these markets, because customers found the delivery time acceptable.

The fastest CJ shipping method typically takes 5 to 11 days when shipping from the US.
It costs more than the standard method.

Use it only when the extra cost is small.
Pay for faster shipping only when the extra cost is small, such as one dollar or a few cents per order.
Do not pay several dollars more per order. It eats up the margin.
Made-to-order products
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t:
Made-to-order products are made after the customer buys.
Set a shipping profile for that supplier that lists the lead time, for example six to eight weeks.

Show the ETA by the add-to-cart button.
Set the same lead time in Merchant Center (Google's product feed tool) (2024).

Made-to-order fulfillment steps (2024):
1. Create a Shopify shipping profile for that supplier. Mark items as custom made, with the lead time.
2. Mirror the same shipping lead time in Merchant Center for that brand.
3. Show a note by the add-to-cart button. It should say the item is made to order, with its ETA.
4. After each sale, **email the customer** to confirm the made-to-order lead time. Do this before the order goes to the supplier.
For freight-shipped products (goods sent by truck, not by parcel), list the shipping method in Google Merchant Center (Google's tool for showing

products in search) as **free shipping at 0 dollars**, not as the freight method (2024).
Google estimates shipping from three things:

**Handling time**: days to get the order ready.
Transit time: days the parcel spends travelling.

Cutoff: the daily order time after which an order counts as the next day.
Google also adjusts the estimate for holidays.
See Handling Time, Transit Time and Delivery Estimates above.
Heavy and freight items
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: For heavy items, **avoid real-time shipping calculation** (the store asks the carrier for a price while the customer shops).
Build the shipping cost into the product price and offer free shipping, if the product still makes a profit.
If real-time shipping is not used for heavy items, a **heavy-item shipping surcharge** (an extra fee for heavy products) can be added automatically on the product page.
For items of **150 to 350 pounds**, the surcharge should match the real shipping cost. Example: $200 extra for a 350-pound item.
Check the surcharge against actual costs.
For a freight-shipped item, use a **freight broker** (a company that books freight for you) through freightcenter.com.
The supplier can provide a freight account (an account with a freight company), or the store can create its own.
Freight shipments should not go through **UPS or FedEx** (parcel delivery companies), because their rates are too high for large items (2024).
If a supplier will not ship on its own account, the store must send **bills of lading** (shipping papers proving the freight was handed to the carrier) for freight shipments (2025).
Freight shipments take **longer** than standard parcels.
Shipping for heavy products can be a **large cost**. Check the shipping cost and label arrangement (how shipping labels are set up) before listing (2024).
See Customs information in Shopify above.
Customs is the government check on goods that cross a border.
Before shipping products from suppliers in other countries to your customers, **ask each supplier** how it handles export (sending goods out of a country) and cross-border shipping,

because the process varies by supplier.
Passing international shipping costs to the buyer is possible only if the **final price** still works for the product.
International UPS shipping is typically **very expensive**. Check the cost with the supplier's calculator before committing.
Shipping policy text
Policy brief (full prompt)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Paste the full brief below into **ChatGPT** (an AI writing tool) or any other AI writing tool. Then add your own answers to the fields at the end.
The result is a finished, professional Shipping Policy (the page that tells customers how orders ship) that can go straight into **Shopify** (the online store platform).
It reads as clear and dependable, and it is tailored to your brand.
The assistant should act as an eCommerce operations copywriter producing a transparent, friendly policy for a Shopify store that sells high-ticket products sourced from domestic suppliers.

The policy should reassure buyers, set realistic delivery expectations, come across as seasoned and reputable, avoid robotic or boilerplate phrasing, and speak to ordinary shoppers rather than legal readers.
The word 'dropshipping' must never appear. Voice: clear, professional, reassuring, trust-building, straightforward.
Format: plain paragraphs under short headers, 300 to 500 words, no filler and no hype, just clarity and confidence.
Required headers, in this order: Shipping Coverage Area, Order Confirmation, Order Processing Time, Shipment Notification & Tracking, Estimated Delivery Time, Shipping Carriers, Delays & Exceptions,
Contact Information. The overall impression should be that of a premium company that treats logistics seriously.
Fields to complete: Store Name [e.g. Coastal Ridge Living]; Support Email Address [e.g. support@coastalrideliving.com]; Shipping Region [e.g. Continental United States only];

Average Handling Time [e.g. 3-5 business days]; Average Transit Time [e.g. 3-7 business days]; Typical Total Delivery Time [e.g. 7-12 business days]; Shipping Partners [e.g. FedEx, UPS, USPS, Freight Carriers];
Do You Ship Freight for Large Items? (Yes/No) [e.g. Yes]; Do You Offer White-Glove or Curbside Delivery?
(Optional) [e.g. Curbside delivery available for oversized items]; How You Handle Out-of-Stock or Custom Orders [e.g. Customer is contacted with updated timelines];
How You Handle Delays [e.g. We proactively notify customers if delays occur].
Closing instructions: build a complete policy that feels established, states delivery timing accurately, earns trust for big-ticket purchases, and can be pasted into Shopify as is.
Each generation should come out differently. Leave out any placeholders, skip explanations and notes, and output only the finished policy. Carry over the field answers exactly as entered.
If the optional field is blank, drop that topic completely rather than inventing details. Return just the ready-to-paste policy copy, with every header alone on its own line.
Building the policy
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Build a Shopify shipping policy for a **high-ticket store** (a store selling expensive items) with domestic suppliers (suppliers in your own country).

Use this order:
1. Shipping Coverage Area
2. Order Confirmation
3. Order Processing Time

4. Shipment Notification & Tracking
5. Estimated Delivery Time
6. Shipping Carriers
7. Delays & Exceptions

8. Contact Information
A high-ticket shipping policy should be **between 300 and 500 words**.
Use simple paragraphs and short section headers. Avoid hype and legal wording.
Write for real customers, so it reads as a premium, established brand that takes logistics (getting orders from you to the buyer) seriously.
A shipping policy pasted into Shopify must not contain **bracketed placeholders** (blank fields in square brackets), notes, or the word "dropshipping".
Leftover template text makes the store look unfinished and damages trust in a high-ticket purchase.
Starting values for the policy's delivery figures are in the **delivery windows table** above.

Use the policy fields to state the **continental United States only** shipping region, plus handling time, transit time and total delivery time, each in business days (working days, not weekends or holidays).
See Claims about speed and Lead times above.
Customers are sensitive to delivery times. Set expectations clearly and keep them **realistic**.
Common Mistakes
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Counting only the advertised shipping days with a supplier **underestimates delivery time**.
Long shipping times can kill viral momentum (sudden fast growth from social media).

Shipping on your own UPS or FedEx account makes you **liable** (responsible) for claims about damaged or lost parcels.
Freight should not go through UPS or FedEx.
Do not have a supplier ship products to **your own address** first and then to the customer. Ask the supplier to ship directly to the customer's address.
**Do not open** a carrier account (an account with a delivery company) before contacting suppliers.
Do not **assume** a group shipping discount is a good deal for everyone.
Do not **assume** shipping on your own account is cheaper without comparing it with **supplier quotes** (price offers).
Ship through the supplier first, since suppliers usually offer the best **shipping rates**.
p.h: Shipping model: supplier account or own account

p.t: If the supplier marks up shipping (adds its own fee on top), ask for better rates or another service.

Then compare quotes from several shipping companies using the same shipment details
Choose products that suppliers can ship on their own account when they allow it.
If an item is damaged or lost, the supplier sends the replacement and handles the **insurance claim** (a request for money back for lost or damaged goods)

If you ship on your own account, you must file the insurance claim yourself.
You then wait to be repaid by the carrier, which is **slower**
Damage is rare. But repeated damage from one supplier's products means that supplier is bad.
Suppliers ideally ship on their own accounts, but some will only ship on yours. This is common

Check this with a **test shipment** (sending one sample order first) before the first order.
Keep a **shipping arrangement table** with one row per supplier, as in the example below.
Check the table **before placing any order**, because it decides whether the supplier or your business books the shipment (arranges pickup and delivery).

**Bobs Brown Chair**: Supplier books shipping
**Super Seats**: We book shipping using UPS
**Crazy Chairs**: Supplier books shipping
Carriers and who books the shipment
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Ask a supplier which **carrier** (delivery company) they use for their top retailers, such as FedEx, UPS, DHL

or a freight broker.
Send shipping details to match that carrier. Ship to the customer's address from the supplier's account
When a supplier arranges shipping, it **books pickup and delivery** with its own nominated carrier (the carrier it chooses) after you place the order.
You only need to pass the customer's delivery address and phone number to the supplier.
For suppliers whose shipping you arrange yourself, ask the supplier for the **package weight and dimensions** before booking, because the carrier needs both.
The supplier sends these details together with its invoice (bill) for the order.
For a supplier with poor shipping and thin margins (little profit left over), **test different warehouse locations and freight companies**.
Add more suppliers with better margins. Those products can then sit in the profitable group that the budget supports
**Free shipping** is the default offer in this dropshipping model, because competitors offer it and customers expect it.
p.h: Free shipping and pricing it in

p.t: The seller does not get shipping for free. The seller pays the supplier and takes on that cost.
Free shipping is offered to customers, and the supplier is paid the actual shipping cost. The store does not calculate shipping through Shopify in this model
Free shipping is offered only to the **continental United States**, not to Alaska, Hawaii or international destinations.
Shipping to those places is very expensive. In other countries, international shipping is usually too costly to offer for free or to make available at all.
Free shipping is an offer many stores overlook.
Shoppers who want to save money will choose a free-shipping store over a similar store that charges delivery.
Free shipping and pricing it in (continued)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: The store can absorb shipping costs to win more customers and stand out from competitors.
Shipping to Canada from US-based suppliers is usually fine with free shipping. But at the start, put most **ad budget** (money spent on ads) into US sales, since those produce the highest profit
Offering free shipping worldwide is only sustainable if the shipping cost is covered by the **product margin** (profit on each sale) or the supplier.

Add the free shipping claim only after checking the cost per country.
Shipping cost limits come from two sources. Both apply to the same goal:
Keep shipping costs at a maximum of **10 dollars**, or make shipping free by building it into the product price. This is especially important for lower-margin products under 50 dollars.
For products under $50, keep shipping at a maximum of about **10%** of the product price. Or offer free shipping by including the shipping cost in the product price.
(Under $50, 10% is at most $5, so the percentage is the tighter limit for those products. The $10 cap is the reference for higher-priced items.)

**Expedited shipping** (fast shipping option) should cost no more than **15-20%** of the product price.
Avoid high expedited fees.
Expedited shipping can be marked up for profit. But only offer it with suppliers who respond **very quickly**
If your supplier usually takes a day or two to respond, a second-day delivery promise puts you in a bad position.
Free shipping and **white glove** (delivery where workers carry the item inside and set it up) can be communicated on the product page, at the product price

and near the **add-to-cart button** (the button that puts the item in the basket)
Showing the estimated arrival date next to free shipping builds trust at the point of purchase.
Ship trial or **free-examination** products (products the buyer can try before paying) from the warehouse or branch nearest the buyer, with shipping paid in advance.

A **shorter delivery distance** shortens the time before the trial starts and keeps the buyer from losing interest.
Prepaid shipping also removes a reason to delay.
Shopify setup: locations, zones, profiles and rates
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Shopify shipping settings must contain at least **one shipping rate** before launch.
A free shipping rate is the minimum required
Shipping must be set up **before launch**, because a shipping zone (a group of countries that share shipping rules) with no rates stops customers in that zone from completing checkout.
The zone shows 'No rates. Customers in this zone won't be able to complete checkout' until at least one rate is added.
Shopify splits shipping into a **Domestic zone** for your home country and an **International zone** that covers the other countries in your active markets (countries you sell to).
Each zone needs at least one shipping rate, because a zone without rates stops checkout for customers located there.
International shipping zones with no rates **block checkout** for those countries.
Shipping rates and active markets must both be in place for each country you want to sell to.
Under Settings > Shipping and delivery, one shipping policy is created for the domestic country, United States, with shipping set to **free**. Free shipping then appears in checkout for US buyers
The location list under Shipping and delivery should contain only the store's own billing address as the **single location**, with everything else left at default.

Supplier addresses should not be added as Shopify locations.
Only the store's own business location belongs there.
Default domestic shipping rates in the example were $7.50 and $5.00. **Delete these default rates** under Settings > Shipping and delivery > General shipping rates before adding your own rates.

Procedure: **Set up shipping rates** in Shopify:
1. Go to Settings > Shipping and delivery and click **Manage** on the shipping profile.

2. Delete the default rates Shopify adds.
3. Create a custom flat rate (one fixed price) named 'Free shipping' with a price of **0**.

4. Add an express option, for example 'Expedited shipping' at $4.99.
5. Repeat for the rest of the world with a suitable rate.
6. Optionally create special zones such as ePacket (a low-cost postal service) or T4 (a budget postal option) for Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom, with their own price.
For a free shipping offer, create a flat rate named for the offer (for example 'Free shipping') with a shipping rate of **0**. Apply it in the zone.
If you offer free shipping to both rate types in the domestic zone, set both to 0.
Shopify setup: locations, zones, profiles and rates (continued)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: For free shipping above a set order value, such as $50, use **'Add conditional pricing'** (a rule that changes the rate based on order value) on the rate instead of a flat 0 rate.
Choose the rate type 'Use flat rate' and enter a custom rate name.
The default package is a 'Sample box' of 22 x 13.7 x 4.2 cm and 0 kg. It is used to calculate shipping rates at checkout.
The Sample box is pre-selected when buying labels, so replace it with your real **package size and weight**.
All products not assigned to another shipping profile go into the **General profile** (the default group of products with shared shipping rules). Newly created products are added there automatically.
Create a new shipping profile only when certain products need different rates or destination restrictions.

Expected delivery date options are **Shop Promise** (Shopify's automated delivery dates for eligible orders), Manual delivery dates (shown for orders without the Shop Promise badge), and Local delivery (off by default,

with a Set up option).
Procedure: **Set up shipping zones** (Settings > Shipping and delivery > General profile):
1. Open the general profile for all products.
2. Create separate zones for the top four markets: Canada, Australia, United States and United Kingdom.

3. Put the remaining countries into a fifth zone. The example lists Germany, Europe, New Zealand and other countries.
4. Add the countries to each zone.
Lumping countries into one zone is acceptable. Separate zones are easier to read and manage.
Procedure: Settings > Shipping and delivery > General profile > Add shipping option for Express Shipping. Choose the Express shipping option and set Rate type to Flat.
Set the price to **$0.00** and enter the number of business days for delivery.
The estimated dates at checkout are calculated from transit time and fulfillment time (time to pack and ship the order).
**Express Free Shipping** is always used. The shipping cost is not charged to the customer. It is instead included in the product price, calculated from the average order value of the bundle sold.

Shipping is therefore set as a flat **$0.00** at checkout.
Shipping rules and shipping costs can be set up later. They do not need to be finished when building the first product page.
Shipping only becomes a detailed task when you add shipping rules or shipping costs
Handling times and dispatch
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Separate processing time from delivery time in the shipping policy.

**Processing** covers how long until the order ships. **Delivery** covers how long until it arrives.
State both as business days.
For an in-stock order (item already on hand), a store can state that it **ships within three business days** of the order date.
The store sends a shipping confirmation within 24 hours after the parcel leaves the warehouse.
If the customer has no shipping confirmation within **four business days**, they can follow up with the store by email.
These timings belong on the shipping page, so customers know the expected window
Some suppliers can **dispatch** (send out the parcel) quickly. CJ Dropshipping (a supplier platform) and similar suppliers can ship orders within about **24 hours** when the product is in stock.
A private agent holding local stock can also ship within 24 hours or less.
A fast dispatch promise can be stated on the store when the supplier is verified to be that quick.
Suppliers such as CJ Dropshipping, or a private agent holding stock, can often dispatch within about 24 hours. This can support a **1-2 day dispatch promise** on the product page.
Confirm dispatch times with the supplier before making that promise.
When the supplier ships within 24 hours, state dispatch time as **'We ship within one to two days'**.
Use the real dispatch time when writing shipping copy. For example, CJ Dropshipping or a private stock agent typically ships within 24 hours or less.
Handling times and dispatch (continued)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Dispatch times differ by source, so use the one your supplier confirms:
In-stock orders with a **3-business-day ship window**, 24-hour confirmation and 4-business-day follow-up
Verified fast suppliers (CJ Dropshipping, private stock agents) at about **24 hours**, supporting a 1-2 day promise
Source D's example template processes orders within **14 business days**.
The template moves orders placed after 12 PM PST (Pacific time), or on weekends or holidays, to the next business day.
This is a template value. Replace it with your supplier's real figure.
Orders are prepared within [X-X] business days, with **weekends and public holidays** not counted.
A confirmation email with tracking details arrives once the parcel has left the store.
Before promising a shipping time or a return window in your policy, **confirm that your supplier can meet it**.
A policy the supplier cannot fulfil creates refund requests and complaints.
Shipping policy text is expected to change after suppliers and products are in place. Delivery times and costs depend on the local shipping area and the country the store operates in
Adjust the shipping page at that point rather than treating the first version as final
Delivery estimates and expectations
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Use the default product template for estimated delivery when all suppliers ship in a similar time.
Create a separate template for each supplier whose delivery window differs, such as one that takes **7 to 14 days**

Show shipping times on the page, for example 7 to 14 days. Mention the express shipping option.
Clear delivery times reduce doubt before the purchase.
Advertising a delivery time you cannot meet leads to complaints and refunds.
Test orders with China-based suppliers reportedly took about **20 days** while quoted 4 to 9 days. So only advertise a delivery time you have measured.
Delivery within about **10 days** is generally acceptable, because customers wait when the product and service are good.

A Prime-like (as fast as Amazon Prime) 1-2 day service only matters at high daily volume from one country.
Express carrier lines come in tiers:

Priority typically delivers in about **3-4 days**.
Standard is the normal choice.
Economy can take 15-18 days.

Delivery of 3-5 days is considered good. Even 5 days is acceptable.
Domestic shipping from a local supplier typically takes **two to four days**.
If a product is on **backorder** (sold out at the supplier and ordered in later), it can take longer
Enter the delivery window in business days based on the fulfillment provider's real transit time.
A **US 3PL** (a third-party company that stores and ships your orders) uses **12 to 21 business days**, or 10 to 14 business days for a faster setup.

A China 3PL needs a longer window because transit is longer.
Do not promise shorter times than the fulfillment center can deliver.

Delivery windows in the sources differ by setup and are not interchangeable:
Source D template: Standard **14 to 21 business days**, Express 7 to 10 business days.

Source C copy template: delivery in 7 to 10 business days.
Source D US 3PL: 12 to 21 business days, or 10 to 14 for a faster setup.
Domestic local supplier: 2 to 4 days
Logistics and customer service matter as much as finding a winning product. Shipping and service failures directly hurt sales and repeat purchases.
Plan these areas **before scaling ad spend** (increasing advertising money).
Delivery estimates and expectations (continued)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: In dropshipping, the supplier ships each order directly to the customer, often from overseas such as China.
Because the store owner cannot control shipping speed, delivery time and working tracking matter a lot for customer trust and repeat purchases.
Shipping times can damage **influencer partnerships** (deals with people who promote your store). Choose suppliers with fast shipping before starting influencer marketing.
Prefer light, non-fragile products (products that do not break easily) when choosing a product.
In one case, **4 kg items** shipped to the UK, Australia and the US without customs problems.
Set the customer-facing delivery window with a positive **lead-in** (an opening sentence). Use this copy on the product page and in checkout (the payment step), replacing bracketed placeholders:
Your order is on its way! We ship your item within [1-2] days, usually within 24 hours, from our [supplier or stock location].
Delivery takes [7-10] business days to your door, and you will receive your tracking number within [12-24] hours of shipping.
Due to high demand, delivery times may vary slightly during peak periods, but we will keep you updated every step of the way.

Open with the positive shipping promise.
Never state a delay without a reassuring line.
Use **'We pay for shipping'** instead of 'free shipping' when shipping is free.

Give the delivery window, such as 7 to 10 business days, with a positive lead-in and tracking within 12 to 24 hours.
Phrase free shipping as **'We pay for shipping'** on the store.
For a holiday promotion that promises delivery before Christmas, the supplier must be able to deliver within about **two weeks**
Confirm this before running the promotion.

Tracking
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: To give customers a local tracking number instead of a China-origin number, follow this procedure.
A tracking number is a code that lets the customer follow their parcel. China-origin means the parcel started in China.
1. **Ask** the supplier or agent to ship with a local carrier. A carrier is the delivery company, such as USPS, Royal Mail or Australia Post. Also ask them to hide the origin information.
2. **Ask** them to send the local number to Shopify automatically once the courier issues it. Shopify is the software your online store runs on.
A courier is the company that delivers the parcel and issues the number.
3. If no local number appears quickly, send the original tracking number and ask them to hide the origin.
The local number often appears the **same day** or within a few hours for destinations like UK, Germany, Australia and New Zealand.
For other destinations, it may only appear when the parcel arrives in the destination country.
A tracking number that covers only the first leg (for example a China number) may not show delivery progress or days left. A leg is one stage of the trip. The local carrier number is needed for that.
Tracking with a local carrier like FedEx or DHL shows the remaining days.
Once an order ships, the customer **receives a tracking number by email** so they can follow the package.
Procedure for Google Merchant Center shipping: Google Merchant Center is Google's tool for showing your products on Google.

1. **Check** the Google Merchant Center shipping settings.
2. **Locate** the free shipping entry. An entry is one line in the settings.
3. **Enter** the average delivery timeframe for the whole catalog. A catalog is your full list of products.
The delivery time applies to the whole catalog, not to each product.
Multi-Supplier and add-On shipments
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: Products sold as **add-ons** or upsells should come from the same supplier as the main product.
An add-on is an extra item sold with the main product. An upsell is an extra offer to buy something more. This way the order ships together without an extra shipping fee.
Items from another source ship separately and need their own handling.

Use a **separate delivery template** for each supplier whose window differs from the default. A delivery template is a saved set of shipping times and rules. A window is the number of days it takes to deliver.
**Record** each supplier's shipping arrangement separately in the table above, because each one may book its own carrier.
**Add shipping insurance** to every shipment. Insurance pays out if a parcel is lost or damaged.
When the supplier ships from its own account, insurance is typically the default. The seller should **confirm it in advance**. An account here is the shipping account used to send the parcel.
Who handles problems depends on whose account is used. A claim is a request for money back from the insurer. A supplier shipping on its own account **handles replacements and claims**.
A store shipping on its own account must **file a claim** and wait for repayment.
When a product ships from **stock in the same country**, the customer pays no extra import fees.
Stock means products kept in a warehouse, ready to ship. Import fees are charges for bringing goods into a country. Customs clearance only matters for cross-border shipments.
Customs clearance is the official check of goods at the border. Cross-border means across a country's border.
For cross-border shipments, carriers such as FedEx, UPS and DHL usually handle customs clearance. They contact the customer when duties must be paid. Duties are taxes on imported goods.
In practice, the **seller typically pays** those fees. Some carriers were not verified for this.
Delivery times can be affected by customs, weather and other factors outside the store's control. Policy means your written store rules.
Customs, duties and cross-Border shipments (continued)
p.s: Shipping setup, policies and delivery expectations

p.t: **Name these factors in your policy.** This sets expectations and reduces complaints about delays.
For international orders where product dimensions vary widely, the store can give shipping prices **on request** rather than publishing one rate. Dimensions means the size of the parcel.
A quote is a price offered for one specific order. The customer confirms the quote before the order and payment are taken. Payment goes through a secure online payment gateway.
A payment gateway is the service that processes card payments. This approach suits low-volume stores, meaning stores with few orders, that cannot yet predict shipping cost per destination.

**Tell customers** that international delivery can take longer than the stated estimate and that you only ship to selected countries. Customers should also receive a tracking number by email once the order ships.
Customers pay customs fees, taxes and import duties on international orders. **Your policy should state this.**
Shipping rates are calculated at **checkout**, based on the customer's location and the shipping option chosen.
Checkout is the final step where the customer pays on your site. The policy should say this, instead of listing fixed prices that may not match the checkout.
